etymology: Greek psychē (ψυχη), “soul, life, breath”; rendered soul, life, and mind in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Psuche is the Greek word of the New Testament for the soul, the life, the inner self of man, and it carries the whole weight of what is at stake in salvation. The Lord Jesus uses it in the most solemn warnings: what is a man profited if he shall gain the whole world and lose his own psuche—his own soul—and what shall a man give in exchange for it? Fear not them which kill the body but are not able to kill the soul; rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. The same word names the life that is laid down and taken up: he that will save his psuche shall lose it, and he that loseth it for Christ’s sake shall find it. It is the soul that magnifies the Lord in Mary’s song, the soul that prospers in John’s blessing, the soul that is the anchor-hold of the believer’s hope. Scripture knows man as body and soul—not a body merely, nor a soul imprisoned in flesh, but an embodied soul created by God, the soul outlasting the death of the body and accountable to its Maker. The dictionary reads psuche as the immortal inner self whose eternal welfare is the chief concern of the gospel: the soul gained or lost forever, worth more than the whole world, redeemed by the blood of Christ.
webster_summary: The Greek word for soul, life, and inner self; the immortal part of man whose eternal welfare—gained or lost—is worth more than the whole world.
webster_full: PSUCHE, Greek for the soul, the life, the inner self of man.

Fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
He that loseth his life for Christ’s sake shall find it.
The immortal soul, accountable to God and worth more than the world.
scriptures: For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?

Luk 1:46
And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord,
Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth.
corruption_summary: Materialism denies the soul outright, and annihilationism denies its immortality; Scripture knows man as an embodied soul, the soul outlasting the body and accountable to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors press against the biblical psuche. The first is materialism, which denies the soul altogether, reducing man to brain and chemistry, so that there is nothing in him to gain or lose, judge or save. The second is annihilationism, which grants a soul but denies its immortality, teaching that the wicked are snuffed out rather than punished forever—against the Lord’s own warning of Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell, and against the everlasting weight His words give to the soul’s gain or loss. If the soul could be gained and lost for an hour only, the bargain of the whole world would not be so terrible.

The principle to recover is the immortal, accountable soul. Man is an embodied soul made by God; the psuche outlasts the death of the body and stands before its Maker. This is why the Lord prizes one soul above the whole world and why the gospel labors for the soul’s eternal welfare. To deny the soul is to empty salvation of its object; to deny its immortality is to dull the urgency of the cross. The believer’s soul magnifies the Lord now and is kept by Him for ever.

etymology: Hebrew bikkurim, “firstfruits,” from the root for the firstborn or first-ripe; the first and best of the harvest given to the LORD.
biblical_def: Bikkurim is the Hebrew word for the firstfruits, the first and best of the harvest, which Israel was commanded to bring to the house of the LORD as an offering of thanksgiving and an acknowledgment that the whole increase came from His hand. The first of the firstfruits of the land was to be brought to the house of the LORD; the worshipper was to honor the LORD with his substance and with the firstfruits of all his increase. The giving of the first portion confessed that God owns all and gives all, and that the part given over consecrates the whole that remains. The Feast of Firstfruits, kept at the beginning of harvest, looked in hope to the full ingathering to come. The New Testament lifts the figure to its height: Christ is risen from the dead and become the firstfruits of them that slept—His resurrection the first sheaf that guarantees the whole harvest of the resurrection of His people. The Spirit given to believers is the firstfruits of the redemption of the body; and the saints themselves are a kind of firstfruits of God’s creatures, begotten by the word of truth. The dictionary reads bikkurim as the offering of the first and best to God in confession that all is His, and as a type fulfilled in the risen Christ, the firstfruits and pledge of the great harvest to come.
webster_summary: The Hebrew word for firstfruits, the first and best of the harvest given to the LORD; fulfilled in the risen Christ, the firstfruits of them that slept.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the prosperity gospel twists firstfruits-giving into a transaction to enrich the giver, against its true sense of glad confession that all is God’s.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse to name is the prosperity gospel’s perversion of firstfruits-giving into a seed-faith transaction—give your first and best to the preacher, and God is obligated to multiply it back to you a hundredfold. This turns a glad acknowledgment that all is God’s into a scheme to enrich oneself, and not seldom to enrich the one who collects. The bikkurim was never a bribe to bend God’s hand but a confession that the increase already came from His; the worshipper honored the LORD with the firstfruits because the LORD had given the harvest, not to leverage a return.

The principle to recover is the consecration of the first and best to God in thankful confession that all is His. The firstfruits given over sanctify the whole that remains and own the Giver of every increase. And the figure is crowned in Christ: He is risen as the firstfruits of them that slept, the first sheaf whose acceptance assures the whole harvest of His people’s resurrection. The Spirit is the firstfruits of our redemption, and the saints a firstfruits of God’s new creation—the first and best, set apart unto Him.

etymology: Hebrew hagah, “to murmur, mutter, moan, meditate”; the word for the low utterance of one pondering the law of God.
biblical_def: Hagah is the Hebrew verb that lies behind the biblical word meditate, and it means far more than silent thought: it is to murmur, to mutter, to ponder aloud in a low voice, the sound of a man turning God’s Word over and over upon his tongue and in his heart. The blessed man of the first Psalm is the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and in His law doth he meditate—hagah—day and night; like a tree planted by the rivers of water, he brings forth his fruit in his season. Joshua was charged to let the book of the law not depart out of his mouth but to meditate therein day and night. The psalmist meditates upon God in the night watches, remembers the days of old and muses on the works of His hands. Biblical meditation is thus the opposite of the emptied mind sought in Eastern and modern practice: it is the filling of the mind with the Word of God, the deliberate, repeated, even murmured chewing of Scripture until it nourishes the soul. The dictionary reads hagah as the appointed exercise of godliness—not vacancy but occupation, not emptying but filling—the believer’s low and constant muttering over the law of his God, the secret of the fruitful and prosperous life.
webster_summary: The Hebrew verb behind “meditate”—to murmur, mutter, ponder aloud; the filling of the mind with God’s Word, the opposite of the emptied mind of false meditation.
webster_full: HAGAH, Hebrew “to murmur, mutter, meditate” on the Word of God.
More than silent thought: pondering Scripture aloud, turning it over and over.
The blessed man meditates in the law of the LORD day and night (Psa 1:2).
Biblical meditation fills the mind; it does not empty it.
The secret of the fruitful and prosperous life.
scriptures: Psa 1:2

corruption_summary: Eastern and modern “meditation” seeks to empty the mind and merge with the divine; biblical hagah fills the mind with God’s Word and fixes it upon His works.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the wholesale replacement of biblical meditation by its Eastern and modern counterfeit. The mindfulness and transcendental practices flooding the West aim to empty the mind, to detach from thought, to dissolve the self into an impersonal divine—the very opposite of hagah. Where the world’s meditation seeks vacancy, Scripture’s seeks occupation; where the one empties, the other fills; where the one merges the self into the All, the other fixes the soul upon the personal God and His revealed Word. To borrow the methods of the emptied mind under the name of meditation is to take a poison for a medicine.

The principle to recover is meditation as the filling of the mind with the Word of God. Hagah is the low, constant murmuring of Scripture, the turning of the law of the LORD over and over until it lodges in the heart; the blessed man does it day and night and is fruitful as a watered tree. The believer meditates on God upon his bed, muses on the works of His hands, talks of His doings—not emptying himself into silence but feeding his soul on the truth. This is the appointed exercise of godliness, and the spring of a prosperous and fruitful walk.

etymology: Hebrew tsedaqah, “righteousness, justice”; conformity to the right standard of God, and the standing of one accounted right with Him.
biblical_def: Tzedaqah is the great Hebrew word for righteousness—conformity to the right standard of God, both the rightness God requires and the standing of one who is accounted right with Him. It is the word of the pivotal text of the gospel in the Old Testament: Abraham believed in the LORD, and He counted it to him for righteousness—tzedaqah reckoned to the believer not by works but by faith, the very seed of the doctrine of justification the apostle Paul would unfold. The word also names the righteousness God demands in the law and the conduct of His people—to do justice and judgment—and in later Hebrew it came to be used of almsgiving, the doing of right by the poor. Yet Scripture is clear that man’s own tzedaqah falls infinitely short: we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. The righteousness that avails before God is His own—the robe of righteousness with which He clothes His people, the righteousness of Christ imputed to the believer who has none of his own. The dictionary reads tzedaqah as the righteousness of God in its double sense: the standard He requires, which fallen man cannot reach, and the gift He gives, reckoned to faith, the imputed righteousness of Christ in which alone the sinner stands accepted.
webster_summary: The Hebrew word for righteousness and justice; both the standard God requires—which fallen man cannot reach—and the righteousness reckoned to faith, fulfilled in Christ’s imputed righteousness.

corruption_summary: Self-righteousness trusts in man’s own tzedaqah, which Scripture calls filthy rags; the righteousness that justifies is God’s gift, reckoned to faith and fulfilled in Christ’s imputed righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The perennial corruption is self-righteousness—the trust in one’s own tzedaqah as the ground of acceptance with God, whether by law-keeping, by ritual, or by good works and almsgiving. But Scripture levels every such hope: all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and by the deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified. To bring one’s own righteousness to God is to bring a polluted thing; the law’s demand of perfect tzedaqah only exposes how far the fallen man falls short. The age that flatters man’s native goodness merely dresses the old self-righteousness in new clothes.

The principle to recover is the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith. Abraham believed, and it was counted to him for righteousness—the pattern of justification, in which God reckons to the believing sinner a righteousness not his own. The robe of righteousness with which God clothes His people is the perfect obedience of Christ, imputed to faith. The tzedaqah that avails before God is His gift, not man’s achievement; the sinner stands accepted not in his own filthy rags but in the spotless righteousness of the Son.

etymology: Hebrew chen, “grace, favor, charm”; the unmerited favor of God or man toward another.
biblical_def: Chen is the Hebrew word for grace or favor—the unmerited kindness shown by a superior to one beneath him, and supremely the gracious favor of God toward sinners. Its first appearance sets the note for all that follows: But Noah found chen, grace, in the eyes of the LORD—found, not earned, in the midst of a generation marked for judgment, the favor that singled out one family for salvation. The word marks Moses, to whom the LORD said, Thou hast found grace in my sight, and I know thee by name, the ground on which Moses dared to plead for the people and to ask to see God’s glory. Chen is the favor the lowly find and the proud forfeit—He giveth grace unto the lowly—and the favor in the sight of God and man that crowns the one who keeps mercy and truth. Always it is unearned: chen is not wages but gift, not a reward for worth but a kindness toward the unworthy. The dictionary reads chen as the Old Testament seed of the great New Testament doctrine of grace: the free, sovereign, unmerited favor of God, found by Noah in a doomed world and by Moses on the mount, poured out at last in fulness through Jesus Christ, of whose fulness we have all received, and grace for grace.
webster_summary: The Hebrew word for grace or favor—the unmerited kindness of God toward sinners; found by Noah in a doomed world, the seed of the New Testament doctrine of grace.

The seed of the New Testament doctrine of free, sovereign grace.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though grace is cheapened into mere divine tolerance or made a wage for worth; chen is free, sovereign favor toward the unworthy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse to name is the cheapening of grace in two opposite directions. On the one hand, grace is flattened into mere divine tolerance—a God who simply overlooks sin because He is too kind to judge—emptying chen of its costly and sovereign character. On the other hand, grace is subtly turned into a wage, a favor God owes to those who have made themselves worthy, so that it ceases to be grace at all. But chen is, from its first appearance, unearned: Noah found grace in a world ripe for the flood, not because he deserved it but because the LORD was gracious to him. Grace that is owed is no grace.

The principle to recover is the free, sovereign, unmerited favor of God. Chen is gift, not wages; kindness toward the unworthy, not reward for the worthy. Noah found it in a doomed generation; Moses found it on the mount; the lowly find it and the proud forfeit it. And what was seed in the Old Testament flowers in the New, where the fulness of grace comes by Jesus Christ, and the sinner is saved by grace through faith, and that not of himself—it is the gift of God, that no man should boast.

etymology: Hebrew kor, the largest dry and liquid measure of Israel, equal to the homer (about six bushels or fifty-five gallons); the Greek koros of the New Testament.
biblical_def: The kor was the largest of the standard measures of ancient Israel, used for grain and for liquids, equal to the homer—some six bushels dry, or about fifty-five gallons—and rendered “measure” in the Authorized Version. It appears in the great quantities of Solomon’s daily provision and of the materials for the temple, and the prophet Ezekiel fixes its value: the kor is an homer of ten baths, for ten baths are an homer. In the New Testament the Greek koros stands behind the hundred measures of wheat in the parable of the unjust steward. As one of the appointed measures of Israel, the kor belongs to the whole biblical witness on weights and measures, in which the LORD requires honesty: a just weight and a perfect measure thou shalt have, for all that do unrighteously are an abomination unto the LORD thy God. A false measure cheats the neighbor and lies before God, who Himself fixed the standards and watches the scales. The dictionary records the kor as a unit of biblical metrology, useful for understanding the scale of temple provision and harvest, and as a standing occasion to remember the LORD’s demand of just measures: the God who appointed the kor and the bath requires that His people give honest measure and abhor the diverse weights of the deceitful.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle the measure presses upon every age is honesty in trade under the eye of God. The kor and the bath were fixed standards, and the LORD bound His people to keep them true: a just weight and a perfect measure thou shalt have; divers weights and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD. The temptation to the false measure—to sell short and buy long, to keep two sets of weights—is as old as commerce and as modern as the marketplace; and it is not a small sin but an abomination, because it cheats the neighbor and lies before the God who watches the scales.

The principle to recover is just measure as a matter of the fear of God. He who appointed the kor and the bath requires that His people give honest measure and abhor the deceitful balance; commerce is conducted before His face, and the merchant’s scales are weighed in heaven. The believer’s integrity in the small matters of weight and measure is a true test of his religion, for he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much, and a false balance is abomination to the LORD.

etymology: Latin denarius, the Roman silver coin worth ten asses; the “penny” of the Authorized Version; Greek dēnarion.
biblical_def: The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin of the New Testament era, worth a day’s wage for a common laborer, and it is the coin the Authorized Version renders “penny”—a value far greater than the modern word suggests. It figures in some of the most familiar scenes of the Gospels. In the parable of the laborers in the vineyard the householder agrees with the workers for a penny a day, and gives the same penny to those who came at the eleventh hour as to those who bore the burden and heat of the day—a picture of the sovereign freedom of grace. When the Pharisees seek to entangle the Lord over tribute, He asks for a penny, points to Caesar’s image and superscription upon it, and answers, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. Two hundred pennyworth of bread would not feed the five thousand; and the good Samaritan left two pence with the host to care for the wounded man. The dictionary records the denarius as the day-wage coin of the New Testament, and notes that knowing its worth opens these passages: the equal penny that magnifies the freeness of grace, the tribute penny that orders the believer’s duty to the magistrate and to God, and the two pence of mercy shown to a stranger.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the KJV “penny” misleads the modern reader; the denarius was a full day’s wage, and knowing this opens the parables.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The point to recover is one of understanding rather than corruption: the Authorized Version’s “penny” misleads the modern ear, suggesting a trifling sum, when the denarius was a full day’s wage for a laborer. To miss this is to miss the force of the passages. The eleventh-hour worker receives a whole day’s pay—a generosity that scandalizes those who bore the heat of the day and magnifies the sovereign freedom of grace, which gives to the late-come the same as to the early. The tribute penny is no token but the real coin of Roman taxation, and the Lord’s answer over it orders the whole question of the believer’s duty to the state.

The principle to recover is the doctrine carried by the coin. The equal penny in the vineyard teaches that God may do what He will with His own, and that grace is His to give freely—the last shall be first. The tribute penny, stamped with Caesar’s image, teaches that the magistrate has his due and God His: render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s. And the Samaritan’s two pence teach that true neighbor-love spends real cost to care for the stranger. The day-wage coin is a small window into great truths.

etymology: Hebrew tophach / tephach, the width of the hand at the base of the fingers, about three inches; the smallest standard measure of length.
biblical_def: The handbreadth was the smallest standard measure of length in ancient Israel, the width of the four fingers at the base of the hand, about three inches, and it serves in Scripture both as a literal measure and as a vivid figure of the brevity of human life. As a measure it fixes dimensions in the tabernacle and temple: the border of an handbreadth around the table of shewbread, the brim of the molten sea an handbreadth thick. As a figure it gives one of the most piercing words on the shortness of our days: Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth, and mine age is as nothing before thee; verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. The psalmist measures the whole span of a life against the eternity of God and finds it no longer than the width of a hand—here and gone, a vapor, a shadow that declineth. The dictionary records the handbreadth as a unit of biblical measure and treasures its great spiritual use: to teach the soul to number its days. Set beside the everlasting God, the longest life is but a handbreadth; and the lesson of the measure is the prayer of Moses—so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom—that the brevity of life might drive the believer to lay hold on the eternal.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age that hides death and dreams of indefinite life forgets the lesson of the handbreadth: that our days are short and must be numbered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson the measure presses is one the present age labors to forget: the brevity of human life. The handbreadth is about three inches; the psalmist makes the whole span of a man as an handbreadth, his age as nothing before God, every man at his best state altogether vanity. The modern world hides death behind hospital walls, distracts the soul with endless amusement, and dreams of indefinitely extended life; and so it forgets to number its days. To live as though life were long is to be a fool with a vapor’s span, building bigger barns while the soul is required.

The principle to recover is the numbering of our short days unto wisdom. The handbreadth measures the longest life against the eternity of God and finds it a hand’s width—here and gone, a shadow that declineth. This is no counsel of despair but of wisdom: so teach us to number our days, prayed Moses, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. The believer who reckons his days a handbreadth lays hold the more firmly on the eternal, redeeming the time, setting his affection on things above, and laboring for the life that does not pass away.

etymology: Greek apostolos (αποστολος), “one sent forth, a messenger, an envoy”; from apostellō, to send away with a commission.
biblical_def: Apostolos is the Greek word for one sent forth—a messenger, an envoy commissioned and authorized by the one who sends him—and it is the source of the title apostle. In its highest and proper use it names the Twelve whom the Lord Jesus chose and sent, with Paul added as one born out of due time, the authorized eyewitnesses of the risen Christ who laid the foundation of the church and through whom the New Testament Scriptures were given. They were sent with His authority, for he that is sent is not greater than he that sent him; and the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone. Remarkably, the word is once applied to Christ Himself: consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus—the One sent by the Father, the great Envoy of God to men. The dictionary holds that the apostolic office, in this foundational sense, was unrepeatable and is now closed: it required being an eyewitness of the risen Lord and bearing His direct commission, and the foundation, once laid, is not laid again. The word may be used in a lower sense of messengers and missionaries sent by the churches, but the office of the apostles of Christ ceased with the apostolic age. The dictionary reads apostolos as the sent one bearing the sender’s authority—supremely the Twelve and Paul, the foundation of the church, and supremely of all, Christ the Apostle of our profession.
webster_summary: The Greek word for one sent forth with authority; the title of the Twelve and Paul, foundational eyewitnesses of the risen Christ—an office now closed—and once of Christ Himself, the Apostle of our profession.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the modern revival of the apostolic office, pressed by the New Apostolic Reformation and kindred movements, which install living “apostles” claiming the authority of the Twelve. But the office of the apostle of Christ, in its proper and foundational sense, was unrepeatable. It required being an eyewitness of the risen Lord and bearing His direct commission—qualifications no man living can meet—and its work was to lay the foundation of the church and to deliver the New Testament Scriptures. A foundation is laid once. To claim apostolic office and authority today is to set a new authority beside the closed canon and to usurp what belonged to the founding age alone.

The principle to recover is the foundational and closed character of the apostolate, and the supremacy of Christ the great Apostle. The church is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ the chief corner stone; that foundation, once laid, abides but is not re-laid. The word apostolos may still describe a messenger sent by the churches, but the office of the apostles of Christ ceased with them. And above all stands the Apostle of our profession, the Son sent by the Father, whose authority the apostles bore and to whom the church looks, having their testimony in the Scripture they left.

etymology: Hebrew Qeren Happuk, “horn of antimony” or “horn of eye-paint”; the name of Job’s third daughter, born after his restoration.
biblical_def: Keren-happuch was the third of the three daughters born to Job after the LORD turned again his captivity and blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. Her name means “horn of antimony” or “horn of eye-paint”—the cosmetic flask of dark powder used to beautify the eyes—and it speaks of beauty and adornment, a fitting name in the household of the man whose grief was now turned to gladness. With her sisters Jemima (“dove” or “daylight”) and Kezia (“cassia,” a fragrant spice), she is named where the sons are not, and Scripture records the singular note that in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job, and that their father gave them inheritance among their brethren—an unusual honor. These are the children of restoration, born on the far side of unimaginable loss, tokens that the God who had given and taken away gave again, doubling Job’s substance and crowning his old age with beauty. The dictionary reads Keren-happuch and her sisters as the quiet seal upon the book of Job: after the whirlwind and the ashes, the LORD blessed the latter end more than the beginning, and the names of the daughters of restoration—beauty, fragrance, and light—tell of the mercy that meets the tried saint at the last.
webster_summary: Job’s third daughter, born after his restoration; her name means “horn of eye-paint,” a token of beauty and of the LORD’s blessing on Job’s latter end.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the restoration of Job is misread as a prosperity-gospel promise of guaranteed earthly reward; it is the sovereign mercy of God to a tried saint.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misreading to guard against is the prosperity-gospel use of Job’s restoration—the daughters of his latter end pressed into a promise that faithful suffering will always be repaid with earthly abundance, health, and beauty. But the book of Job is the great rebuke of exactly that mechanical reckoning: his comforters insisted that suffering must mean hidden sin and that righteousness must bring reward, and the LORD declared they had not spoken of Him what was right. Job’s doubled blessing is sovereign mercy, not a wage owed; many a faithful saint, like the heroes of Hebrews 11, died without receiving the promises, awaiting a better resurrection.

The principle to recover is the sovereign goodness of God to the tried, who gives and takes away and is blessed in both. Keren-happuch and her sisters are the children of restoration, tokens that the God who met Job in the whirlwind also crowned his old age with beauty and light; their lovely names—eye-paint, cassia, dove—tell of mercy after mourning. Yet the lesson is not that godliness guarantees a doubled estate, but that the latter end of the saint is in the hand of a faithful God, whose mercies, in this life or the next, are sure to all who trust Him.
